metadata.title: Mapping student engagement in creative thinking: An explainable machine learning approach to behavioral heterogeneity

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 creative thinking process data (computer-based assessment) combined with student questionnaire contextual variables for three economies (Canada, Germany, Hong Kong). The analytic sample is restricted to students with valid cases in the three economies and further filtered for predictive modeling by removing variables with >30% missingness and imputing remaining missing values. The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) in the ML training/evaluation pipeline. Because the models are XGBoost classifiers trained on a train/test split with SMOTE and class weighting, the authors’ approach appears to rely on unweighted ML estimation; readers should treat performance metrics as descriptive/predictive rather than fully population-representative unless weights are confirmed in the supplementary materials.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: plausible_values_handling is 'not_applicable' — the study likely does not analyze cognitive achievement PVs (e.g., it may focus on affective/attitudinal outcomes, curriculum data, or non-ILSA micro-data).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses PISA 2022 creative thinking computer-based assessment process data and student questionnaire contextual data. For clustering, it extracts valid cases from the three economies (Canada, Germany, Hong Kong) and derives four process features per item (scored response/credits, action count, orientation time, processing time). Disengaged behaviors are identified using PISA criteria for task disengagement (rapid responding, relative rapid responding, non-responding) and the P+>0% method; remaining cases are transformed into z-scores for k-means clustering. For predictive modeling, students are classified as disengaged vs engaged based on whether their most common multi-task patterns are all disengaged behaviors; variables with missingness >30% are deleted, and remaining missing values are imputed via hot-deck KNN. The paper also notes that in Canada, 10 cases were deleted due to too few completed tasks and missing mode.task-level and individual-level factors.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (process data; predictive engagement/disengagement; Canada)
main_findings.performance_metrics: XGBoost classifier (with LASSO feature selection; SMOTE + class weighting; 80/20 split; 10-fold CV on training for hyperparameters). Canada: Accuracy=0.92, Precision=0.93, Recall=0.92, F1=0.93, Specificity=0.96, AUC=0.75.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking data (process data with contextual questionnaire variables; Canada), the study leveraged self-reported effort, work in household, reading and mathematics achievement, and creative self-efficacy to predict engagement vs disengagement, finding that the XGBoost model achieved strong classification performance (e.g., F1=0.93 and AUC=0.75). This indicates that combining behavioral engagement traces with core academic competence and self-efficacy measures can help identify students at risk of disengagement in creative tasks, though the study’s SHAP-based interpretability is predictive rather than causal and survey-weight use is not reported.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (process data; predictive engagement/disengagement; Germany)
main_findings.performance_metrics: XGBoost classifier (with LASSO feature selection; SMOTE + class weighting; 80/20 split; 10-fold CV on training for hyperparameters). Germany: Accuracy=0.91, Precision=0.92, Recall=0.92, F1=0.92, Specificity=0.96, AUC=0.79.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking data (process data with contextual questionnaire variables; Germany), the study leveraged mathematics and reading achievement, mathematics self-efficacy, arriving late for school, and mother occupational status to predict engagement vs disengagement, finding that the XGBoost model performed well (e.g., F1=0.92 and AUC=0.79). This indicates that engagement in creative tasks is strongly linked to both academic competence and motivational/behavioral readiness indicators, suggesting that targeted supports (e.g., strengthening self-efficacy and addressing attendance-related behaviors) may reduce disengagement risk, while cross-cultural non-linearities revealed by SHAP should not be interpreted as causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (process data; predictive engagement/disengagement; Hong Kong)
main_findings.performance_metrics: XGBoost classifier (with LASSO feature selection; SMOTE + class weighting; 80/20 split; 10-fold CV on training for hyperparameters). Hong Kong: Accuracy=0.87, Precision=0.87, Recall=0.87, F1=0.87, Specificity=0.93, AUC=0.78.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking data (process data with contextual questionnaire variables; Hong Kong), the study leveraged science and reading achievement, parents’ expectations, distress from online cyberbullying, and stress resistance to predict engagement vs disengagement, finding that the XGBoost model achieved good performance (e.g., F1=0.87 and AUC=0.78). This indicates that both academic foundations and psychosocial stress-related factors are important for sustaining engagement in creative tasks, implying that schools and families may need coordinated interventions addressing stress and online harms alongside learning supports, while the study’s predictive explanations remain non-causal.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2022 creative thinking computer-based assessment process data (plus student questionnaire context) for three economies—Canada, Germany, and Hong Kong—to (i) identify engagement/disengagement patterns across multiple creative tasks via k-means clustering and (ii) predict whether students are mostly engaged or disengaged using supervised ML. Disengagement is operationalized using PISA task disengagement indicators (rapid responding, relative rapid responding, non-responding) and the P+>0% method, and predictive modeling uses LASSO feature selection followed by XGBoost classification with SMOTE and class weighting to address engagement (~95%) vs disengagement (~5%) imbalance. Missing values are handled by deleting variables with >30% missingness and applying hot-deck KNN imputation. Across economies, the best XGBoost models reach Accuracy/F1 of 0.92/0.93 (Canada), 0.91/0.92 (Germany), and 0.87/0.87 (Hong Kong), with AUC ranging from 0.75 to 0.79. SHAP dependence plots reveal non-linear and threshold relationships, but these are interpretive associations rather than causal effects, and the manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling/replicate weights in the ML pipeline.
